lessons.title: Quadrilaterals, regular polygons and circles
lessons.summary: Classify quadrilaterals, use regular symmetry and connect the circumference to the diameter.
lessons.objective: Classify quadrilaterals, use regular symmetry and connect the circumference to the diameter.
lessons.before: Use properties to sort shapes, rather than judging how a drawing looks.
lessons.ideas:
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Rectangles add four right angles. Rhombuses add four equal sides. A square has both extra properties.

For n sides there are n lines of symmetry and n matching positions during a full turn. The smallest positive turn angle is 360° divided by n.

The ratio of circumference to diameter is constant. It is π. Use C = πd or C = 2πr.
lessons.method:
If two family names work, give the most specific one when asked.

Give a numerical angle only when the question asks for an angle.

Write the exact π form before rounding an approximate value.
mistakes: A tilted square is still a square.
The order counts positions, not degrees.
Check whether the given length is a radius or a diameter.

examples.title: A design made from a regular polygon
examples.question:
A regular 21-sided sign turns about its centre.

  1. Give its order of rotational symmetry.

    [2]

  2. Find the smallest positive angle of rotation that leaves the sign unchanged.

    [2]

  3. How many lines of symmetry does this sign have? Explain.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each of the 21 sides can move to the position of the first side and the polygon still matches.

\(21\)

(b) One full turn is \(360^\circ\). Split it into 21 equal moves.

\(\frac{120}{7}\) degrees

(c) Each vertex is equally spaced around the centre. A regular polygon has one symmetry axis for each of its sides in total.

\(21\)

examples.title: Measuring around a circular cover
examples.question:
A circular pond cover has radius \(\frac{41}{2}\) m.

  1. Give the circumference to two decimal places.

    [2]

  2. Write the circumference exactly in terms of π.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The diameter is twice the radius, so it is \(41\) m. Multiply the diameter by π.

Use the calculator π key and round just the final result.

\(128.81\) m

(b) Circumference divided by diameter is π for every circle. Multiply the diameter by π.

\(41\pi\) m

lessons.title: Areas and distance conversions
lessons.summary: Calculate areas of parallelograms and trapezia, and convert between miles and kilometres.
lessons.objective: Calculate areas of parallelograms and trapezia, and convert between miles and kilometres.
lessons.before: Cut a right triangle from one end of a parallelogram and move it to the other end.
lessons.ideas:
The cut makes a rectangle with the original base and perpendicular height. Its area is their product.

The new base is the sum of the two parallel sides. Multiply that sum by the perpendicular height, then halve.

Multiply miles by 1.6 for kilometres. Divide kilometres by 1.6, or multiply by 5/8, for miles.
lessons.method:
Use square units for area.

Show the formula with the values substituted.

Check whether the number should grow or shrink.
mistakes: A sloping side is not the height unless it meets the base at a right angle.
Only add the parallel side lengths in the trapezium area formula.
Changing units leaves the actual distance unchanged.

examples.title: Finding the area of a sloping panel
examples.question:
A parallelogram has a 8 cm base and a 5 cm sloping side. The perpendicular height above its base is 3 cm.

  1. Find the area of the panel.

    [2]

  2. Find the perimeter of the panel.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Slide a right triangle from one end to the other to make a rectangle. The base and perpendicular height are unchanged.

The rectangle has dimensions 8 cm by 3 cm.

\(24\) cm²

(b) Opposite sides are equal. For perimeter use the actual side lengths.

\(26\) cm

examples.title: Area of a trapezium
examples.question:
A flower bed forms a trapezium with parallel sides 7 m and 9 m. They are 5 m apart at right angles.

  1. Find the area of the flower bed.

    [2]

  2. Explain what the height in the area formula means.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Two identical copies form a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the parallel sides. Take half of its area.

Multiply 16 by 5, then halve the result.

\(40\) m²

(b) This distance makes a right angle with both parallel sides.

The shortest distance between the parallel sides.

examples.title: Miles and kilometres
examples.question:
An outdoor route is 155 miles long. Use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km.

  1. Give the approximate length in kilometres.

    [2]

  2. Convert a different route of \(256\) km to miles using the same conversion.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) One mile corresponds to 1.6 kilometres, so multiply the count of miles by 1.6.

\(248\) km

(b) To reverse the conversion, divide the kilometres by 1.6.

\(160\) miles

lessons.title: 3D views, area and volume
lessons.summary: Read orthographic views and work with the faces, surface area and volume of solids.
lessons.objective: Read orthographic views and work with the faces, surface area and volume of solids.
lessons.before: A face is a flat surface. An edge joins two faces. A vertex is a corner.
lessons.ideas:
For a convex polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2. Count each shared edge only once.

Calculate half the triangle’s base times its perpendicular height. Multiply the end area by the length of the prism. For surface area add all five face areas.

Add the areas of all outside faces. A pyramid has a base and a triangle for each base edge. Use the height measured on the triangular face.

Front shows width and height. Side shows depth and height. Top shows width and depth. Use the same scale throughout.
lessons.method:
Write V − E + F = 2 before substituting.

Write cm³ for volume and cm² for surface area.

Check the count of outer faces before adding their areas.

Name the direction and label the scale for each view.
mistakes: A hidden edge is still an edge of the solid.
The prism length and the triangle height are different lengths.
A hidden face still contributes to the total. The vertical height inside a pyramid is different from its face height.
A 3D perspective drawing is different from a straight-on view.

examples.title: Count a prism’s faces, edges and vertices
examples.question:
A prism has two identical 6-sided ends and one rectangular face for each side of an end.

  1. Work out the number of vertices.

    [2]

  2. Use Euler’s relation to find the number of edges.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are 6 vertices at each of the two ends.

\(12\)

(b) Count the two ends and the 6 rectangular faces to get 8 faces.

For this solid, vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2. Use 12 plus 8 minus 2.

\(18\)

examples.title: Volume of a triangular prism
examples.question:
A prism has length 8 cm. Its identical triangular ends are right-angled, with the two perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm.

  1. Work out the volume.

    [2]

  2. Work out the surface area. The third side of each triangle is 5 cm.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The area of an end is one half of 3 × 4, which is 6 cm².

Repeat this cross-section along the 8 cm length.

\(48\) cm³

(b) The two triangles total 12 cm². The three rectangular faces have widths 3, 4 and 5 cm.

Multiply the widths by 8 cm and add the triangular area.

\(108\) cm²

examples.title: Finding the outside area of a box
examples.question:
A closed cuboid of dimensions 9 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm needs wrapping.

  1. Find the total area of its six faces.

    [2]

  2. How could you label a net to show what you counted?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The front and back each have area 27 cm². The top and bottom each have area 18 cm². The two side faces each have area 6 cm².

\(102\) cm²

(b) A net shows all outer faces, including those hidden in a perspective drawing.

Label two rectangles with each matching pair of dimensions, 9 × 3, 9 × 2 and 3 × 2.

examples.title: Drawing views of a storage box
examples.question:
A cuboid is 6 cm wide, 8 cm high and 2 cm deep.

  1. Find the height on its front view when the drawing uses 2 mm for each centimetre.

    [2]

  2. Give the dimensions of the top and side views at the same scale.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A straight-on front view keeps width and height. Multiply the real height in centimetres by 2 to get the drawing height in millimetres.

\(16\) mm

(b) The top view keeps width and depth. The side view keeps depth and height.

Top: 12 mm by 4 mm. Side: 4 mm by 16 mm.
